videos.title: Why this course uses ML, optimization and Python
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, pp. 4–5, 23–26 and 33–36
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Why this course uses ML, optimization and Python. You run an ice-cream shop and want to make better business decisions. First inspect last year's daily sales. You cannot trust a prediction if the rows contain mistakes. Use ML to predict possible demand, then choose stock quantities subject to storage, cost and spoilage constraints. Python lets you read the data and check both calculations; it does not replace the business question. A common mistake is: A model's prediction is not automatically an optimal business decision. Quick check: Which ability is an explicit aim of the course? The correct answer is: Recognise and check what code and models do.

content.hook: What should you be able to check independently at the end of the course?
content.scenario: You run an ice-cream shop and want to make better business decisions.
steps: First inspect last year's daily sales. You cannot trust a prediction if the rows contain mistakes.
Use ML to predict possible demand, then choose stock quantities subject to storage, cost and spoilage constraints.
Python lets you read the data and check both calculations; it does not replace the business question.
content.plainEnglish: Your goal is not to memorise generated code. You should recognise which business problem is being solved, inspect data, understand the procedure, question results and connect predictions to decisions. The course moves from cleaning raw data to supervised methods, unsupervised methods and optimization. Practice and the lecture exercise notebooks are central to this learning-by-doing approach.
content.university: Machine learning makes inferences from examples; optimization chooses an action under constraints. Python notebooks let you implement and audit both. Lecture 1 also previews the course sequence, participation expectations, homework, a midterm and a final. Administrative details are not substitutes for the current official course page.
content.math: raw data → cleaned data → analytical model → checked insight → decision
content.trap: A model's prediction is not automatically an optimal business decision.
content.quiz: Which ability is an explicit aim of the course?
content.correctAnswer: Recognise and check what code and models do

videos.title: What is machine learning?
videos.source: Lecture 1, slides 7–17
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand What is machine learning?. A shop keeps a table of yesterday's temperature and ice creams sold. Each past day is an example. Temperatures and sales are observed together. A learning algorithm estimates a relationship from those examples. It has not been handed a rule for every possible day. Give it a new temperature to make an estimate, then test it on days it did not learn from. A common mistake is: A fixed thermostat rule is not automatically machine learning just because it runs on a computer. Quick check: A spam filter learns from examples marked spam. What kind of task is it? The correct answer is: Supervised ML.

content.hook: How can a computer learn patterns without being told every rule?
content.scenario: A shop keeps a table of yesterday's temperature and ice creams sold.
steps: Each past day is an example. Temperatures and sales are observed together.
A learning algorithm estimates a relationship from those examples. It has not been handed a rule for every possible day.
Give it a new temperature to make an estimate, then test it on days it did not learn from.
content.plainEnglish: Machine learning studies examples to detect patterns that help us predict new information. Instead of writing every rule by hand, we give a program examples, let it learn a rule and test whether the rule works on unseen examples.
content.university: A model is a function learned from observed data. A model's parameters are estimated using a training algorithm. Assess its generalization on examples it has not trained on.
content.math: data → learning algorithm → fitted model → new prediction
content.trap: A fixed thermostat rule is not automatically machine learning just because it runs on a computer.
content.quiz: A spam filter learns from examples marked spam. What kind of task is it?

videos.title: Supervised, unsupervised, optimization
videos.source: Lecture 1, slides 7–17
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Supervised, unsupervised, optimization. A bank needs to predict defaults, understand customer groups and allocate a lending budget. Supervised: use historical loans with known default outcomes to predict which new loans may default. Unsupervised: examine customer characteristics without a known outcome to find useful groupings. Optimization: choose a loan portfolio under budget and risk constraints. A prediction helps, but does not choose the portfolio. A common mistake is: Don't assume any use of numbers or rules is ML. Quick check: Which activity directly chooses the best route under limits? The correct answer is: Optimization.

content.hook: What's the difference between predicting and deciding?
content.scenario: A bank needs to predict defaults, understand customer groups and allocate a lending budget.
steps: Supervised: use historical loans with known default outcomes to predict which new loans may default.
Unsupervised: examine customer characteristics without a known outcome to find useful groupings.
Optimization: choose a loan portfolio under budget and risk constraints. A prediction helps, but does not choose the portfolio.
content.plainEnglish: Supervised learning has a known answer called a label. Unsupervised learning searches for patterns without answers attached. Optimization chooses the best action while respecting rules and constraints. A prediction can inform a decision, but the two are not identical.
content.university: Supervised learning maps features X to target y. Unsupervised methods use X without y. Optimization maximizes/minimizes an objective over feasible choices.
content.math: supervised: X → y | unsupervised: X → structure | optimization: choose best feasible action
content.trap: Don't assume any use of numbers or rules is ML.
content.quiz: Which activity directly chooses the best route under limits?

videos.title: What does ‘AI’ actually mean?
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, pp. 18–20 (definitions and AI-or-not-AI comparisons)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand What does ‘AI’ actually mean?. A company advertises an 'AI-powered' bank assistant. Ask what it actually does: follow fixed rules, learn from examples, generate text or choose an action? Compare the underlying task to the definitions being used; definitions of AI are not identical. Don't judge an algorithm by a marketing label. Ask for inputs, outputs and validation. A common mistake is: Do not infer from the term 'AI' that a product learns, predicts, optimizes or complies with a particular law. Quick check: What question best tests an AI marketing claim? The correct answer is: Which actual algorithm and evidence are behind it?.

content.hook: Does adding the word AI to a product prove it uses a particular algorithm?
content.scenario: A company advertises an 'AI-powered' bank assistant.
steps: Ask what it actually does: follow fixed rules, learn from examples, generate text or choose an action?
Compare the underlying task to the definitions being used; definitions of AI are not identical.
Don't judge an algorithm by a marketing label. Ask for inputs, outputs and validation.
content.plainEnglish: No. Artificial intelligence is a broad label, and its meaning depends on the definition being used. A chatbot, fraud detector, thermostat and route planner may be classified differently under different definitions or regulations. In this course, machine learning and optimization are treated as more precisely defined ideas. Ask what input, model and action are actually involved.
content.university: The lecture compares classifications under the EU AI Act, an ISO standard and marketing descriptions. These definitions do not necessarily include the same technologies. A technology's commercial label should not be treated as evidence of its computational method or legal status.
content.math: AI is a broad category; ML and optimization are better-defined tools
content.code:
claim = 'AI-powered forecasts'
print('What data, model and validation support this claim?')
content.trap: Do not infer from the term 'AI' that a product learns, predicts, optimizes or complies with a particular law.
content.quiz: What question best tests an AI marketing claim?
content.correctAnswer: Which actual algorithm and evidence are behind it?

videos.title: Generative AI versus LLMs
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, p. 21 (Generative AI and LLMs)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Generative AI versus LLMs. A shop uses software to forecast demand and another tool to draft a customer email. Demand prediction estimates a number. It may use ML without producing creative content. Generative AI creates content; a language model can generate the email's text. Check both outputs. Being fluent in language does not mean the email's facts are true. A common mistake is: An LLM-written explanation or code snippet still needs to be checked for factual and programming errors. Quick check: Which statement is most accurate? The correct answer is: LLMs are an example of generative AI.

content.hook: Is an LLM the same thing as all of AI?
content.scenario: A shop uses software to forecast demand and another tool to draft a customer email.
steps: Demand prediction estimates a number. It may use ML without producing creative content.
Generative AI creates content; a language model can generate the email's text.
Check both outputs. Being fluent in language does not mean the email's facts are true.
content.plainEnglish: No. Generative AI produces new content such as text, images or code from patterns learned in existing material. A large language model, or LLM, is a language-focused generative model, especially associated with generating text. Not every AI application is generative, and not every generative AI model is an LLM.
content.university: The lecture introduces generative AI as a family of content-producing models and LLMs as a prominent example. It notes that LLM development can involve supervised and reinforcement learning methods. This lecture introduces rather than fully teaches these methods.
content.math: Generative AI ⊃ text-generating LLMs (as a class)
content.trap: An LLM-written explanation or code snippet still needs to be checked for factual and programming errors.
content.quiz: Which statement is most accurate?
content.correctAnswer: LLMs are an example of generative AI

videos.title: Python building blocks
videos.source: Lecture 1, Python recap and notebook
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Python building blocks. You want a Python cell to calculate a 10% price increase. Put the original price in a variable, for example price = 100. Calculate price * 1.1; the result is 110. Variables store values, not equations to solve. Use print() to see the value. Use == to compare values; = performs assignment. A common mistake is: An equals sign assigns a value; == tests whether two values are equal. Quick check: What is printed by print(2 ** 3)? The correct answer is: 8.

content.hook: What does Python code actually do when it runs line-by-line?
content.scenario: You want a Python cell to calculate a 10% price increase.
steps: Put the original price in a variable, for example price = 100.
Calculate price * 1.1; the result is 110. Variables store values, not equations to solve.
Use print() to see the value. Use == to compare values; = performs assignment.
content.plainEnglish: Variables are named containers for values. A string is text, a float is a decimal number, an integer is a whole number, and a Boolean is True or False. Python reads statements in order, evaluates expressions and stores results.
content.university: Assignments use =; comparisons use ==, < and >; ** means exponentiation. A function call uses parentheses. Square brackets may identify a list or select items from an object.
content.trap: An equals sign assigns a value; == tests whether two values are equal.
content.quiz: What is printed by print(2 ** 3)?

videos.title: Google Colab, imports, operators and Python types
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, pp. 31–38 (Google Colab and Python recap)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Google Colab, imports, operators and Python types. You open a new Google Colab notebook to work with a table. Run an import cell such as import pandas as pd; now pd is the package's short name. Create an integer count and a decimal price, then multiply them. Run cells in a sensible order. Variables from a cell do not exist until that cell has run. A common mistake is: The order in which cells are executed affects available variables; rerun from the top when the environment is inconsistent. Quick check: Which operation raises 2 to the third power in Python? The correct answer is: 2 ** 3.

content.hook: What happens before you can use pandas or NumPy in a notebook?
content.scenario: You open a new Google Colab notebook to work with a table.
steps: Run an import cell such as import pandas as pd; now pd is the package's short name.
Create an integer count and a decimal price, then multiply them.
Run cells in a sensible order. Variables from a cell do not exist until that cell has run.
content.plainEnglish: Google Colab runs Python inside notebook cells. A package provides existing functions; an import brings the package into your current Python session. Python has values of different types: integers, decimals, text and Booleans. '+' adds, '/' divides, '**' raises to a power and '#' starts a comment. Execute prerequisite cells before using their variables.
content.university: Using 'import pandas as pd' binds a short alias to a module. Notebook state depends on which cells you have run, not merely their visual order. Packages may already be installed in Colab, but imported names still need to be defined.

videos.title: Comparisons, if/else and for loops
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, p. 39 (comparison, conditionals and for loops)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Comparisons, if/else and for loops. An analyst must flag fares that are less than zero. The comparison fare < 0 produces either True or False. An if branch prints 'invalid' for negative fares. else handles the others. A for loop repeats that check for each fare; indentation groups statements. A common mistake is: Python uses '==' for comparison and '=' for assignment. Indentation is meaningful. Quick check: Which statement checks if fare is negative? The correct answer is: if fare < 0:.

content.hook: How can code make a choice or repeat work?
content.scenario: An analyst must flag fares that are less than zero.
steps: The comparison fare < 0 produces either True or False.
An if branch prints 'invalid' for negative fares. else handles the others.
A for loop repeats that check for each fare; indentation groups statements.
content.plainEnglish: Comparison operators ask whether something is true: '==', '!=', '>=', '<='. 'if' checks a condition and chooses a branch; 'else' handles another case. A 'for' loop repeats a block for each item in a list. Indentation tells Python which statements belong together.
content.university: Conditional flow and iteration let a program implement simple data validation and transformations. Pandas operations may replace explicit loops for table work, but reading basic conditions and loops is essential for interpreting notebook code.
content.trap: Python uses '==' for comparison and '=' for assignment. Indentation is meaningful.
content.quiz: Which statement checks if fare is negative?

videos.title: Pandas, NumPy and plotting
videos.source: Lecture 1 Python notebook; Lecture 3 exercise Part 1

An array stores values efficiently for calculations. Selecting one predictor column as a two-dimensional table gives 13 rows and 1 feature: shape (13, 1). content.hook: What is a DataFrame, and why does its shape matter?
content.scenario: You have 13 days of ice-cream observations and one predictor: time.
steps: A DataFrame is a spreadsheet-like table. An array stores values efficiently for calculations.
Selecting one predictor column as a two-dimensional table gives 13 rows and 1 feature: shape (13, 1).
A scatterplot displays each day's observation, while a fitted line is a separate model result.
content.plainEnglish: A DataFrame is a table of rows and columns. A NumPy array is a collection of numbers that Python can calculate with efficiently. Matplotlib turns values into charts. A column from a DataFrame can be one-dimensional (Series) or two-dimensional (DataFrame).
content.university: The .shape property gives (rows, columns). In regression, X usually has shape (n_samples, n_features) and y has one value per sample. Example: 13 rows and one feature gives X.shape = (13, 1).

import pandas as pd

videos.title: Matplotlib plots and chart labels
videos.source: Lecture 1 handout, p. 40 (plotting recap)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Matplotlib plots and chart labels. Plot three sales observations across three days. Use a scatterplot when you want to see separate observed points. Label horizontal axis as Day and vertical axis as Sales so the chart has interpretable units. Use a line for a trend or connected series, and a histogram for the distribution of a single numerical variable. A common mistake is: A chart without labelled axes makes it easy to misread units or confuse categories and quantities. Quick check: Which function plots each observation as a separate point? The correct answer is: plt.scatter().

content.hook: What do plot(), scatter() and hist() help you see?
content.scenario: Plot three sales observations across three days.
steps: Use a scatterplot when you want to see separate observed points.
Label horizontal axis as Day and vertical axis as Sales so the chart has interpretable units.
Use a line for a trend or connected series, and a histogram for the distribution of a single numerical variable.
content.plainEnglish: A line plot connects measurements; a scatterplot shows individual data points; a histogram groups values into ranges. Plot labels and titles explain what an axis measures. Always inspect whether you're looking at observations, model predictions or both before interpreting a curve.
content.university: Matplotlib's pyplot interface includes plt.plot, plt.scatter, plt.hist, plt.xlabel, plt.ylabel, plt.title and plt.show. Appropriate chart type depends on the structure of the observations and the question, and chart conventions should not be mistaken for causal evidence.
content.math: X-axis = predictor; Y-axis = target (for a basic regression plot)
content.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.scatter([1,2,3],[5,7,6])
plt.xlabel('Day')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.title('Three sales observations')
plt.show()
content.trap: A chart without labelled axes makes it easy to misread units or confuse categories and quantities.
content.quiz: Which function plots each observation as a separate point?

videos.title: The raw-data-to-insight pipeline
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 2–4 (learning objectives and ML pipeline)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand The raw-data-to-insight pipeline. A raw Titanic CSV is about to become a prediction dataset. Check raw rows and column meaning first; do not start by choosing an algorithm. Preprocessing fixes wrong values and missing entries, yielding prepared data. Feature engineering builds useful numerical/categorical predictors. Only then do models produce insights. A common mistake is: Do not start tuning algorithms before verifying what the rows and columns actually mean. Quick check: What normally happens before feature engineering? content.hook: Why do business datasets need preparation before modelling?
content.scenario: A raw Titanic CSV is about to become a prediction dataset.
steps: Check raw rows and column meaning first; do not start by choosing an algorithm.
Preprocessing fixes wrong values and missing entries, yielding prepared data.
Feature engineering builds useful numerical/categorical predictors. Only then do models produce insights.
content.plainEnglish: Machine learning begins with raw records, not model code. Preprocessing catches invalid or missing values. Feature engineering transforms the cleaned records into useful model inputs. Only then can modelling create insights. The correct steps depend on what each business variable represents.
content.university: The lecture's process is raw data → data preprocessing → prepared data → feature engineering → engineered features → modelling → insights. Inspection and domain expertise govern each transition.
content.math: raw data → cleaned data → engineered features → modelling → insights

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('Titanic.csv')

content.trap: Do not start tuning algorithms before verifying what the rows and columns actually mean.

videos.group: 1. Inspect raw data and identify variable types
videos.title: Titanic observations and variable types
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 5–7 (Titanic dataset and variable types)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Titanic observations and variable types. You inspect a table where each row is one Titanic passenger. One row is one observation. Age and Fare record numerical quantities. Pclass may be stored with numbers, yet represents ordered passenger classes. Survival is an outcome label for a future classification task. Do not confuse label with input features. A common mistake is: Treating Pclass 3 as three times Pclass 1 is not justified merely by the codes. Quick check: Which Titanic column represents a category despite a possible numeric code? The correct answer is: Pclass.

content.hook: Can a column containing numbers still be categorical?
content.scenario: You inspect a table where each row is one Titanic passenger.
steps: One row is one observation. Age and Fare record numerical quantities.
Pclass may be stored with numbers, yet represents ordered passenger classes.
Survival is an outcome label for a future classification task. Do not confuse label with input features.
content.plainEnglish: Yes. An observation is one passenger, while a feature is a recorded characteristic. The lecture's Titanic dataset contains 893 rows and 11 features. Age and Fare are numerical measurements; Pclass is a category represented by a code even if displayed as a number; Sex is also categorical. A label such as survival is the outcome a future model would predict.
content.university: Numeric values express measurements or counts; categorical values express group membership. Ordinal categories have an order, while nominal categories do not. Python's dtype alone does not determine the business meaning of a variable.
content.math: n observations × p features; Titanic source: 893 × 11
content.trap: Treating Pclass 3 as three times Pclass 1 is not justified merely by the codes.
content.quiz: Which Titanic column represents a category despite a possible numeric code?

videos.group: 1. Inspect raw data and identify variable types
videos.title: Rows, columns and data quality
videos.source: Lecture 2, slides 5–15
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Rows, columns and data quality. A passenger table has ages, ticket classes, fares and ports. Rows are passengers; columns are recorded features. Check shape, types and examples. An impossible negative fare suggests corrupt data; a missing age is a different issue. Decide which columns carry real information before cleaning them. A common mistake is: An unusual number isn't always an error. Investigate true outliers rather than deleting them automatically. Quick check: What should you do before training on a new dataset? The correct answer is: Inspect types and strange values.

content.hook: Why can one wrong number spoil the analysis?
content.scenario: A passenger table has ages, ticket classes, fares and ports.
steps: Rows are passengers; columns are recorded features. Check shape, types and examples.
An impossible negative fare suggests corrupt data; a missing age is a different issue.
Decide which columns carry real information before cleaning them.
content.plainEnglish: Each row is an observation. Each column is a feature. Missing, duplicate or impossible values can mislead a model. Start by inspecting .head(), .info(), .describe() and .isna().sum() before fitting anything.
content.university: EDA (exploratory data analysis) establishes types, ranges, cardinality, distribution and missingness. A numerical-looking category such as passenger class may be categorical even when represented by 1, 2 or 3.
content.trap: An unusual number isn't always an error. Investigate true outliers rather than deleting them automatically.
content.quiz: What should you do before training on a new dataset?

videos.group: 1. Inspect raw data and identify variable types
videos.title: Inspect a DataFrame before cleaning
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 5, 10 and 13 (head, info, describe, unique)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Inspect a DataFrame before cleaning. You suspect the Embarked column contains an unexpected port code. head() lets you inspect a few rows; info() checks data types and missing entries. describe() highlights suspicious numerical ranges such as negative fares. unique() shows unexpected text categories. The output tells you where to investigate, not what to delete automatically. A common mistake is: df.describe() mainly summarises numerical columns by default; it will not expose every problematic text category. Quick check: Which operation is most useful for finding unusual text categories? The correct answer is: df['Embarked'].unique().

content.hook: How can you find bad values without staring at every row?
content.scenario: You suspect the Embarked column contains an unexpected port code.
steps: head() lets you inspect a few rows; info() checks data types and missing entries.
describe() highlights suspicious numerical ranges such as negative fares.
unique() shows unexpected text categories. The output tells you where to investigate, not what to delete automatically.
content.plainEnglish: Use df.head() to preview rows; df.info() to inspect columns, types and non-missing counts; df.describe() to summarise numerical columns; and df['column'].unique() to examine categories and unexpected spellings. These operations help identify where to investigate, not automatically decide what to delete.
content.university: Diagnostic methods identify value distributions, object dtypes, missing entries and potentially impossible records. A sound audit also checks duplicates and category frequencies, while retaining the original dataset for reproducibility.
content.math: data audit = types + missingness + ranges + categories
content.trap: df.describe() mainly summarises numerical columns by default; it will not expose every problematic text category.
content.quiz: Which operation is most useful for finding unusual text categories?

videos.title: Invalid values and outlier diagnosis
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 9–13 (invalid data, outliers and Titanic example)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Invalid values and outlier diagnosis. A passenger's Fare is negative, while another's Fare is unusually high. Negative fare may be impossible in this dataset: inspect and correct or remove the corrupt record. An unusually high fare might reflect a genuine first-class ticket. Boxplots and z-scores flag candidates for investigation, not automatic deletion. A common mistake is: Do not delete every observation whose z-score exceeds 3; the underlying distribution and business context matter. Quick check: Which is a suitable reason to investigate a Titanic Fare entry? The correct answer is: Fare is negative.

content.hook: Is every extreme data point a mistake that must be removed?
content.scenario: A passenger's Fare is negative, while another's Fare is unusually high.
steps: Negative fare may be impossible in this dataset: inspect and correct or remove the corrupt record.
An unusually high fare might reflect a genuine first-class ticket.
Boxplots and z-scores flag candidates for investigation, not automatic deletion.
content.plainEnglish: No. A negative passenger Fare is suspicious because a fare should not be negative. But a very expensive fare might be real. Use summary statistics and filters to find invalid records. Outliers can be explored using boxplots, z-scores or anomaly detectors; use business knowledge to distinguish mistakes from unusual but genuine observations.
content.university: The handout uses a corrupt Titanic record in row 892 as an example for filtering and dropping. It distinguishes erroneous entries from legitimate extremes and introduces boxplots, z-score magnitudes above 3, and anomaly detection as ways to flag—not prove—outliers.
content.code:
bad = df[df['Fare'] < 0]
print(bad)
# Drop only confirmed corrupt rows after inspection
content.trap: Do not delete every observation whose z-score exceeds 3; the underlying distribution and business context matter.
content.quiz: Which is a suitable reason to investigate a Titanic Fare entry?

videos.title: Duplicate rows and uninformative features
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 13–15 (non-informative features and duplicates)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Duplicate rows and uninformative features. A dataset appears to contain two identical passenger rows. Check whether the duplicate is a repeated import or two legitimate entries. drop_duplicates removes exact repeated rows; deleting a name shared by two people is not the same task. A column with the same value in every row gives no discrimination; a random identifier may also be unhelpful. A common mistake is: Two passengers may share a name or ticket; duplicate names are not the same as duplicate rows. Quick check: Which check tests whether complete rows repeat? The correct answer is: df.duplicated().

content.hook: Why can duplicated or meaningless columns mislead a model?
content.scenario: A dataset appears to contain two identical passenger rows.
steps: Check whether the duplicate is a repeated import or two legitimate entries.
drop_duplicates removes exact repeated rows; deleting a name shared by two people is not the same task.
A column with the same value in every row gives no discrimination; a random identifier may also be unhelpful.
content.plainEnglish: Duplicate observations can over-weight a repeated record. Columns that are constant for every row provide no variation, while purely arbitrary unique identifiers may add no useful information. The lecture introduces dropping rows/columns, checking duplicates and removing confirmed non-informative features.
content.university: Pandas supports duplicated() and drop_duplicates() for repeated records, and drop(columns=...) for fields. Do not remove unique identifier columns automatically: some identifiers carry meaningful grouping or linkage information. Make removal decisions using domain knowledge.
content.math: number of unique values = 1 → constant feature
content.trap: Two passengers may share a name or ticket; duplicate names are not the same as duplicate rows.
content.quiz: Which check tests whether complete rows repeat?

videos.title: Missing values and imputation
videos.source: Lecture 2, slides 18–22, exercise Part 1
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Missing values and imputation. Several passengers have no recorded age. Count missing ages with isna().sum() before deciding how to fill them. You might replace a missing age with a median, use similar passengers or keep an 'unknown' marker. Missing-data strategies can change the data distribution and should be justified. A common mistake is: Always distinguish unknown from real zero. Avoid fitting an imputer on all samples before a model evaluation split. Quick check: What should an imputer learn its parameters from? The correct answer is: Train data only.

content.hook: Why is filling blank cells with zero often wrong?
content.scenario: Several passengers have no recorded age.
steps: Count missing ages with isna().sum() before deciding how to fill them.
You might replace a missing age with a median, use similar passengers or keep an 'unknown' marker.
Missing-data strategies can change the data distribution and should be justified.

videos.title: MCAR, MAR and MNAR: why data goes missing
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, p. 21 (three missing-data mechanisms)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand MCAR, MAR and MNAR: why data goes missing. Some form fields were left blank for different reasons. MCAR: a field may be absent for reasons unrelated to values under study. MAR: missingness can depend on other observed features, such as age group. MNAR: missingness relates to the missing value or unobserved factors. Simple imputation may introduce serious bias. A common mistake is: Missingness is not always innocuous. Do not automatically replace every gap with an overall average. Quick check: Which type can depend on other recorded variables? The correct answer is: MAR.

content.hook: Can missingness itself contain information?
content.scenario: Some form fields were left blank for different reasons.
steps: MCAR: a field may be absent for reasons unrelated to values under study.
MAR: missingness can depend on other observed features, such as age group.
MNAR: missingness relates to the missing value or unobserved factors. Simple imputation may introduce serious bias.
content.plainEnglish: Yes. Missing completely at random (MCAR) has no systematic relationship to observed or unobserved values. Missing at random (MAR) can depend on other observed features. Missing not at random (MNAR) can depend on the missing value itself or factors not accounted for, making repair harder. These mechanisms affect whether simple replacement is trustworthy.
content.university: Distinguish MCAR, MAR and MNAR conceptually: 'at random' in MAR does not mean there is no pattern; it means the mechanism may be explained by observed data, conditional on those variables. The handout notes MNAR can be harder to mitigate and may benefit from more features.
content.math: MCAR: independent; MAR: related to observed data; MNAR: related to missing/unseen factors
content.trap: Missingness is not always innocuous. Do not automatically replace every gap with an overall average.
content.quiz: Which type can depend on other recorded variables?

videos.title: Numerical missing values: delete, estimate or impute
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 18–19 and 22 (numerical imputation)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Numerical missing values: delete, estimate or impute. You need an age value for a row with Age missing. First check how many ages are absent and whether missingness follows any pattern. Simple options include deleting the row or imputing a training-set mean/median. More advanced options use similar passengers or prediction models. They may preserve useful patterns but add assumptions. A common mistake is: Replacing every missing age with one value erases natural variation; evaluate the consequences for the task. Quick check: Which method uses other passengers' attributes to estimate a missing age? The correct answer is: Nearest-neighbour imputation.

content.hook: How might you fill an unknown passenger age?
content.scenario: You need an age value for a row with Age missing.
steps: First check how many ages are absent and whether missingness follows any pattern.
Simple options include deleting the row or imputing a training-set mean/median.
More advanced options use similar passengers or prediction models. They may preserve useful patterns but add assumptions.
content.plainEnglish: First identify the missing cells. Options include dropping rows or a mostly empty column, replacing missing numbers with mean/median or extrema, finding similar observations and using their value, sampling from neighbours, or estimating a value with regression. More sophisticated methods can incorporate uncertainty. Pick the method based on the business problem.
content.university: The handout moves from simpler methods to nearest-observation and regression-based imputation. For Titanic Age, it demonstrates estimating from similar observations and using sklearn.impute. For a reliable pipeline, learn imputers only from training rows and retain a missingness indicator when informative.
content.math: mean imputation: missing Age ← training-set mean Age

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
imputer = SimpleImputer(strategy='median')
# Fit on observed ages in the training split
content.trap: Replacing every missing age with one value erases natural variation; evaluate the consequences for the task.
content.quiz: Which method uses other passengers' attributes to estimate a missing age?

You can also drop affected rows or use similar records to predict the category. In Titanic, the lecture proposes filling missing Embarked with the most frequent 'S', while dropping Cabin because too many values are missing.

videos.source: Lecture 2, slides 16–17; optional preprocessing reading
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Scaling and encoding. One feature measures fares and another records ages. Very different scales can affect distance-based methods and numerical stability. Min-max normalization rescales a training range to approximately 0–1; standardization centres at zero with unit standard deviation. A decision tree often does not need scaling, while some linear, distance and PCA workflows benefit. content.hook: How can 0–1 values and 0–100,000 values coexist in one model?
content.scenario: One feature measures fares and another records ages.
steps: Very different scales can affect distance-based methods and numerical stability.
Min-max normalization rescales a training range to approximately 0–1; standardization centres at zero with unit standard deviation.
A decision tree often does not need scaling, while some linear, distance and PCA workflows benefit.
content.plainEnglish: Standard scaling subtracts a column's mean and divides by its standard deviation; min-max scaling maps the training data's observed range, usually to 0–1. One-hot encoding converts categories into separate 0/1 columns. These transformations create model-ready numerical inputs.
content.university: Scaling helps algorithms that are sensitive to feature magnitudes; tree methods often do not require it. Use Pipeline to ensure training-fitted transformations are applied consistently to validation and test data.

videos.title: Min-max normalization versus standard scaling

content.scenario: Two columns have very different units: Fare and Age.
steps: Min-max uses the minimum and maximum learned from training rows.
StandardScaler subtracts training mean and divides by training standard deviation.
Apply the SAME learned transformation to validation and test data; do not recalculate their own scales.
content.plainEnglish: A Fare measured in tens of currency units and an Age measured in years use different ranges. Min-max normalization often maps a chosen training range into 0 to 1; standard scaling centres a feature around mean 0 and scales it to standard deviation 1. Some models benefit, but a decision tree typically does not need the same scaling.
content.university: The lecture uses 'normalizing' for min-max [0,1] and 'scaling' for standardization (mean 0, standard deviation 1), and mentions regressions/PCA versus trees. Later, the proper supervised pipeline should fit preprocessing statistics on training data only.

# Fit on training rows only when a supervised split exists

videos.title: Ordinal encoding versus one-hot encoding
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, pp. 24–25 (ordinal, nominal and one-hot encoding)
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Ordinal encoding versus one-hot encoding. You want to model Titanic embarkation port and passenger class. Passenger class has an order; a deliberate ordinal encoding can preserve it. Ports S, C and Q have no inherent numeric ranking. Give them separate dummy columns instead. For a linear model with an intercept you can omit one dummy as a reference category. A common mistake is: An integer label for a nominal category can accidentally imply meaningful distance between categories. Quick check: Which feature is nominal in the lecture example? The correct answer is: Embarked.

content.hook: Why should different categories be encoded differently?
content.scenario: You want to model Titanic embarkation port and passenger class.
steps: Passenger class has an order; a deliberate ordinal encoding can preserve it.
Ports S, C and Q have no inherent numeric ranking. Give them separate dummy columns instead.
For a linear model with an intercept you can omit one dummy as a reference category.
content.plainEnglish: Some categories have a meaningful order, like first/second/third class. Others, such as departure ports S, C and Q, do not have an intrinsic ranking. Ordinal encoding assigns codes in an intended order; one-hot encoding makes separate 0/1 indicator columns. Sometimes one redundant one-hot column is dropped.
content.university: The lecture contrasts Pclass (ordinal) with Embarked (nominal) and illustrates one-hot coding plus a dropped redundant column. For linear regression with an intercept, including all category dummies may cause perfect multicollinearity; dropping one provides a reference category.
content.math: Embarked=S → [1,0]; C → [0,1]; Q → [0,0] when Q is reference
content.code:
import pandas as pd
ports = pd.DataFrame({'Embarked':['S','C','Q']})
print(pd.get_dummies(ports, columns=['Embarked']))
content.trap: An integer label for a nominal category can accidentally imply meaningful distance between categories.
content.quiz: Which feature is nominal in the lecture example?

videos.title: Convert numbers into categories using bins
videos.source: Lecture 2 handout, p. 26 (numerical-to-categorical binning)

Pick age boundaries, for example under 30, 30–49 and 50+ as illustrative cutoffs. Assign each age to its corresponding band; this creates a new categorical variable. Binning is simpler to interpret but loses differences among people within one band. A common mistake is: A histogram already has bins, but choosing category cutoffs can erase information near a boundary. Quick check: Which operation converts numerical ages into age groups? The correct answer is: Binning.

content.hook: When might exact numerical detail be less useful than a range?
content.scenario: You want a high-level age-band chart rather than exact ages.
steps: Pick age boundaries, for example under 30, 30–49 and 50+ as illustrative cutoffs.
Assign each age to its corresponding band; this creates a new categorical variable.
Binning is simpler to interpret but loses differences among people within one band.
content.plainEnglish: Binning or bucketization groups continuous or count values into ranges such as age bands. Each bin becomes a category and can be summarised, counted or used as a transformed feature. Choose boundaries intentionally; information may be lost when distinct values fall in the same bin.
content.university: The handout introduces numerical-to-categorical conversion through bucketization and aggregation. In pandas, cut() supports specified boundaries and qcut() supports quantile-based groups, but their behaviour differs with repeated values and boundaries.

ages = pd.Series([18,27,42,63])
labels = pd.cut(ages, bins=[0,29,49,120], labels=['Young','Middle','Older'])

Feature selection keeps some of the original columns and drops others. Dimension reduction constructs a smaller set of new combined dimensions. Lecture 2 previews the distinction; detailed dimensionality reduction belongs later in the course. content.scenario: A table has 100 columns but you want a simpler model.
steps: Feature selection keeps some of the original columns and drops others.
Dimension reduction constructs a smaller set of new combined dimensions.
Lecture 2 previews the distinction; detailed dimensionality reduction belongs later in the course.
content.plainEnglish: No. Feature selection picks a useful subset of existing features. Dimension reduction creates fewer new dimensions that combine information from multiple old features. steps: Combine SibSp + Parch + 1 to form an illustrative family-size count.
A transform changes one column; for example a logarithm or unit conversion.
An interaction deliberately uses two variables together, such as multiplying or adding features.

Interactions combine information from multiple features, such as passengers' siblings/spouses and parents/children travelling together. These can help a model represent relationships it could not express using only the original columns.

The lecture mentions converting a 1912 Fare into today's euros and combining Parch and SibSp. Any conversion needs a defined exchange/inflation assumption rather than an invented fixed multiplier.

videos.source: Lecture 3, slides 4–9

The output of interest is a number, so regression is a candidate. You collect examples with known input values (days/times) and actual sales. content.hook: You own an ice-cream shop. How many ice-creams will you sell tomorrow?
content.scenario: An ice-cream shop wants to know tomorrow's sales.
steps: The output of interest is a number, so regression is a candidate.
You collect examples with known input values (days/times) and actual sales.
A model learns an approximate relationship and estimates new sales. The estimate is not a certainty.
content.plainEnglish: Regression is a type of supervised learning used when the answer we want is a NUMBER. Given examples with inputs and known outputs, the model learns a relationship to estimate new outputs. In Gelato, Time (day in a year) is an input; Sales is the target. Classification instead answers with categories, such as 'rain' or 'no rain'.

videos.title: Supervised learning: regression or classification?

Predicting a passenger's age is predicting a number: regression. Predicting whether that passenger survived is predicting a category: classification. An outcome encoded as 0 or 1 is still categorical if you are predicting which class it belongs to. A common mistake is: Do not decide regression versus classification solely from whether the label is stored as an integer. Quick check: Predicting if a passenger survived is generally which task? content.hook: How do you know whether a prediction should be a number or category?
content.scenario: Two Titanic problems sound similar but need different outputs.
steps: Predicting a passenger's age is predicting a number: regression.
Predicting whether that passenger survived is predicting a category: classification.
An outcome encoded as 0 or 1 is still categorical if you are predicting which class it belongs to.
content.plainEnglish: In supervised learning, each example has a known target (label). Regression predicts a number such as sales or price. Classification predicts a category such as survived/not survived. Before choosing a model, write down the target and decide what kind of answer it has.
content.university: The output type frames the model and evaluation: a numerical target suggests regression metrics, while a categorical target suggests classification methods and metrics. A binary label represented as 0/1 is still a category if the task is to identify a class.
content.math: numeric target → regression; categorical target → classification
content.trap: Do not decide regression versus classification solely from whether the label is stored as an integer.

Times is the predictor X; Sales is the target y you want to estimate.

steps: Put the day or time on the horizontal axis and sales on the vertical axis.
Each dot represents one actual observation, not a model output.

videos.group: 1. Supervised regression and the Gelato linear model
videos.title: Slope, intercept and predictions
videos.source: Lecture 3, slides 10–14
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Slope, intercept and predictions. Suppose a fitted line is y = 200 - 0.5x (illustrative coefficients). The intercept 200 is the prediction when x is zero, not automatically an observed sale. The slope -0.5 means a one-unit increase in time changes the predicted sales by -0.5 under that line. For x = 10, the line predicts 195. This is a hypothetical arithmetic example, not the Gelato fit. A common mistake is: The intercept may not be meaningful when x=0 is outside the observed range. Quick check: For ŷ = 10 + 4x, what is ŷ when x = 3? The correct answer is: 22.

content.hook: What do the two numbers in a straight-line equation mean?
content.scenario: Suppose a fitted line is y = 200 - 0.5x (illustrative coefficients).
steps: The intercept 200 is the prediction when x is zero, not automatically an observed sale.
The slope -0.5 means a one-unit increase in time changes the predicted sales by -0.5 under that line.
For x = 10, the line predicts 195. This is a hypothetical arithmetic example, not the Gelato fit.
content.plainEnglish: A linear regression line has an INTERCEPT (starting height) and a SLOPE (how much the predicted outcome changes when x increases by one unit). In ŷ = 20 + 3x, if x is 2, the prediction is 26. If slope is negative, predictions fall as x rises. These numbers describe association in the model, not necessarily a causal effect.
content.university: The fitted relation is ŷ = β₀ + β₁x. β₀ is the predicted value at x=0; β₁ is the fitted change in ŷ per unit x, holding other regressors constant when present.

content.hook: How does a model choose a line without guessing?
content.scenario: Two students draw different lines through the same sales dots.
steps: An eyeballed line depends on a person's judgement.
Fitting chooses a model's parameters using a specified rule on the observed data.
A good-looking training fit is not enough: it must generalise to unseen observations.
content.plainEnglish: You can draw any line through points, but the computer chooses the line that minimizes a defined measure of disagreement between actual and predicted values. In ordinary least squares, that means minimizing the sum of squared residuals. The slope and intercept are learned from the examples.
content.university: Ordinary least squares estimates coefficients β by minimizing Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)². This is a convex problem in the linear coefficients, so there is a least-squares optimum when appropriate identifiability conditions hold.

The predicted value is 110. Residual = actual minus predicted = +10 for that day. Residual size and direction describe error; one residual cannot establish the model's future accuracy. A common mistake is: Residuals have a sign; absolute error removes the sign; squared error penalizes big misses more. Quick check: Actual is 50, predicted is 65. Residual? The correct answer is: −15.

content.hook: How wrong was each prediction?
content.scenario: On one day the shop sold 120 ice creams, but the line predicted 110.
steps: The actual value is 120. The predicted value is 110.
Residual = actual minus predicted = +10 for that day.
Residual size and direction describe error; one residual cannot establish the model's future accuracy.
content.plainEnglish: A residual is the difference between what actually happened and what the model predicted. If a shop sold 120 ice-creams but the model predicted 100, the residual is +20. If it predicted 130, the residual is −10. Residuals above and below zero indicate different directions of error.
content.university: eᵢ = yᵢ − ŷᵢ. Inspect residual-versus-prediction plots to detect systematic curvature, changing spread and extreme errors. Residuals from training data are not a substitute for testing on new data.
content.trap: Residuals have a sign; absolute error removes the sign; squared error penalizes big misses more.
content.quiz: Actual is 50, predicted is 65. Residual?

videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Why squares? Ordinary least squares. A candidate line misses three sales observations by 2, -3 and 1. Square the misses: 4, 9 and 1; the total squared error is 14. Ordinary least squares searches for coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals. Squaring makes all contributions nonnegative and penalises larger misses more strongly. A common mistake is: Because errors are squared, MSE is not measured in the original units. RMSE is. Quick check: Which error matters more in squared-error loss? The correct answer is: 10-unit error.

content.hook: Why not just add all errors together?
content.scenario: A candidate line misses three sales observations by 2, -3 and 1.
steps: Square the misses: 4, 9 and 1; the total squared error is 14.
Ordinary least squares searches for coefficients that minimise the sum of squared residuals.
Squaring makes all contributions nonnegative and penalises larger misses more strongly.
content.plainEnglish: Positive errors and negative errors can cancel out. Squaring makes every error positive and gives large misses extra weight. Ordinary least squares finds the slope and intercept that make the total squared error as small as possible. A single big miss can influence that fitted line quite strongly.
content.university: SSE = Σ(y−ŷ)². MSE = SSE/n and measures average squared error in squared units; differentiating the least-squares objective yields normal equations, though libraries generally solve the fit numerically.

mse = mean_squared_error(y, model.predict(X))
content.trap: Because errors are squared, MSE is not measured in the original units. RMSE is.

steps: Dots are the actual sales. The line shows the model's prediction at each time.
Look at vertical gaps: large gaps imply greater residual error.
Check whether the gaps change with time; a curved pattern could indicate a missing nonlinear relationship.

An array like [1,29,60] is one-dimensional: shape (3,). Reshaping to (3, 1) makes three observations and one feature column. The notation (-1,1) asks NumPy to infer the number of rows while keeping one column. steps: An array like [1,29,60] is one-dimensional: shape (3,).

A scikit-learn model with one feature expects a 2D input: one row for each day, one column for Times. steps: intercept_ gives the fitted constant term and coef_ gives feature slopes.
score(X,y) gives the coefficient of determination R² for that evaluated dataset.

videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand DataFrame names, warnings and safe predictions. A model fitted with DataFrame columns receives a bare array at prediction time. Column names and order are part of the information given during fitting. Feeding differently named or reordered inputs can produce errors or wrong interpretations. Pass the same feature names and order to predict() that the model was fitted to expect. A common mistake is: The new_data columns must match the training features. A warning is not always the same as an exception. Quick check: What is the best prediction input after training on a DataFrame with column Times? content.hook: Why do I sometimes get a warning even when my code works?
content.scenario: A model fitted with DataFrame columns receives a bare array at prediction time.
steps: Column names and order are part of the information given during fitting.
Feeding differently named or reordered inputs can produce errors or wrong interpretations.
Pass the same feature names and order to predict() that the model was fitted to expect.
content.plainEnglish: If you train with a pandas DataFrame named Times, scikit-learn remembers the feature name. Calling predict([[100]]) supplies a plain list without names; some versions warn that valid feature names are missing. A clearer habit is to predict using a DataFrame with the same column names and order as training. The input shape must remain (rows, columns).
content.university: Use the same feature schema in training and inference. Where possible, construct X_new = pd.DataFrame({'Times':[100]}) and call model.predict(X_new). When training on NumPy arrays, apply that choice consistently instead. Library warnings are useful clues about input schema, not necessarily fatal errors.

predicted_sales = model.predict(new_day)
print(predicted_sales)
content.trap: The new_data columns must match the training features. A warning is not always the same as an exception.

videos.title: Five methods you must recognise
videos.source: Lecture 3 pipeline and scikit-learn documentation supplement
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Five methods you must recognise. A notebook shows fit, transform, fit_transform, predict and score. fit learns parameters from a dataset, such as regression coefficients or scaling statistics. transform changes the representation using learned preprocessing; fit_transform does both steps on training rows. predict produces outputs for given inputs; score evaluates a defined metric, which varies by estimator. A common mistake is: Never fit a scaler on the test data. score() measures whatever the specific estimator documents, not one universal metric. Quick check: Which operation uses an already-learned scaler without relearning its statistics? The correct answer is: transform(X_test).

content.hook: What is the difference between fit, fit_transform, transform, predict and score?
content.scenario: A notebook shows fit, transform, fit_transform, predict and score.
steps: fit learns parameters from a dataset, such as regression coefficients or scaling statistics.
transform changes the representation using learned preprocessing; fit_transform does both steps on training rows.
predict produces outputs for given inputs; score evaluates a defined metric, which varies by estimator.
content.plainEnglish: fit() learns parameters from training inputs (and targets where applicable). transform() applies a learned transformation to inputs. fit_transform() learns and transforms the input, normally on training data only. predict() uses a fitted estimator to estimate targets. score() evaluates performance using features and known targets; for LinearRegression it returns R-squared. Memorise their roles, then check which object each method belongs to.
content.university: Transformers such as StandardScaler learn statistics during fit and apply them with transform. Estimators such as LinearRegression learn coefficients during fit and use them in predict. Pipeline sequences preprocessing and estimators, handling transformations consistently during cross-validation and inference.
content.math: fit = learn | transform = change inputs | predict = estimate outputs
content.code:
scaler.fit(X_train)
X_train_scaled = scaler.transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)
model.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)
predictions = model.predict(X_test_scaled)
content.trap: Never fit a scaler on the test data. score() measures whatever the specific estimator documents, not one universal metric.
content.quiz: Which operation uses an already-learned scaler without relearning its statistics?

videos.title: R-squared: what does it tell us?
videos.source: Lecture 3 exercise Part 2; mathematical supplement
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand R-squared: what does it tell us?. You compare a fitted line with always predicting the average sale. R² describes the relative reduction in squared error versus that mean-only baseline on the same evaluation set. R² = 1 indicates a perfect fit; 0 means no improvement over the baseline; negative means worse. An in-sample R² can be optimistic; a test-set R² is more informative about generalisation. A common mistake is: Do not confuse R² with accuracy, probability of correctness or causal importance. Quick check: What does R² = −0.2 on a test set mean? The correct answer is: Worse SSE than a test-set mean baseline.

content.hook: Does R² = 0.9 mean 90% of forecasts are right?
content.scenario: You compare a fitted line with always predicting the average sale.
steps: R² describes the relative reduction in squared error versus that mean-only baseline on the same evaluation set.
R² = 1 indicates a perfect fit; 0 means no improvement over the baseline; negative means worse.
An in-sample R² can be optimistic; a test-set R² is more informative about generalisation.
content.plainEnglish: No. R² tells us how much better the model's squared-error fit is compared with predicting the mean, for the dataset being evaluated. An R² of 0 means no improvement over that baseline on the evaluated sample. It can be negative on a test set. It is NOT the percentage of predictions that are correct.
content.university: R² = 1 − Σ(y−ŷ)² / Σ(y−mean(y))², provided the target is not constant. Interpreted as variance explained in specific in-sample OLS conditions, but not an automatic measure of prediction quality in all settings.
content.trap: Do not confuse R² with accuracy, probability of correctness or causal importance.
content.quiz: What does R² = −0.2 on a test set mean?
content.correctAnswer: Worse SSE than a test-set mean baseline

videos.title: Polynomial regression
videos.source: Lecture 3, slides 16–22; notebook Part 3
videos.oneMinuteNarration: Here is a simple way to understand Polynomial regression. Sales rise and fall during the year, so a straight trend is too rigid. A linear model uses a straight line: a + bx. A polynomial expands the input into x, x², x³ and so on, then fits coefficients with linear regression. More flexible curves can follow seasonal data better, but very high degree may fit noise. A common mistake is: A higher degree does not prove better forecasting. Standardise/normalise x for numerical stability in high-degree cases. Quick check: What new feature appears in degree-2 polynomial regression? The correct answer is: x² only alongside lower terms.

content.hook: What if the data bend instead of moving in a straight line?
content.scenario: Sales rise and fall during the year, so a straight trend is too rigid.
steps: A linear model uses a straight line: a + bx.
A polynomial expands the input into x, x², x³ and so on, then fits coefficients with linear regression.
More flexible curves can follow seasonal data better, but very high degree may fit noise.
content.plainEnglish: Polynomial regression adds columns such as x² and x³, then fits coefficients using ordinary linear regression. In scikit-learn, PolynomialFeatures includes a column of ones by default; LinearRegression also fits an intercept by default. This redundancy is handled numerically, but include_bias=False is cleaner for a new pipeline. Degree 2 can create a U-shaped curve; degree 3 can bend again. Polynomial regression is still LINEAR IN ITS COEFFICIENTS, even though the curve bends in x.
content.university: Construct basis features [1,x,x²,...,x^d]. Fit a linear regression over the transformed columns. The model family gains flexibility as d increases, but also greater risk of fitting noise.

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=2)
X_poly = poly.fit_transform(X)
model = LinearRegression().fit(X_poly, y)
content.trap: A higher degree does not prove better forecasting. Standardise/normalise x for numerical stability in high-degree cases.
content.quiz: What new feature appears in degree-2 polynomial regression?

A common mistake is: Always apply the TRAINING-FITTED scaler to held-out examples. Quick check: What happens to 365^12 relative to 0.5^12? The correct answer is: It is much larger.

content.hook: Why do high powers of calendar day cause numerical trouble?

steps: x to a high power becomes a very large number, which can hurt numerical stability.
Rescaling or using better-conditioned polynomial representations can help.
Fit numerical preprocessing on training rows and apply the same transformation to test rows.

content.scenario: A straight line misses a clearly curved sales pattern.
steps: The model is too restrictive to represent the underlying shape.
Even on the training data, predictions miss the main structure.
This is underfitting: increasing useful model flexibility may help.
content.plainEnglish: Underfitting means the model cannot capture an important pattern. Ice-cream sales rise and fall seasonally, but a straight line can only slope up or down. This produces systematic errors even on training data. Try a model flexible enough to capture the important structure.

videos.source: Lecture 3 overfitting, polynomial activity

Training error can become extremely small because the curve follows specific observations. Small changes in the sample may give a very different curve and poor future forecasts. This is overfitting: use validation, simpler models and caution about extrapolation. A common mistake is: Perfect training fit is not sufficient evidence of useful prediction. content.hook: Why isn't a curve through every dot automatically great?
content.scenario: A degree-12 curve winds through every one of 13 sales dots.
steps: Training error can become extremely small because the curve follows specific observations.
Small changes in the sample may give a very different curve and poor future forecasts.
This is overfitting: use validation, simpler models and caution about extrapolation.
content.plainEnglish: Overfitting is learning quirks of your training examples that don't repeat in new examples. With just 13 Gelato days, a degree-12 curve may wiggle through nearly every point but produce unreasonable new forecasts. The training score can improve while validation performance worsens.
content.university: As flexibility increases, training MSE generally decreases while out-of-sample error may increase. Use properly separated evaluation sets to choose complexity; with 13 examples, any single split is very uncertain.

content.trap: Perfect training fit is not sufficient evidence of useful prediction.
